task: Rewrite this issue body so a reader with no context understands it. Keep every fact.
draft:
## Overview

In today's fast-paced data landscape, robust backups are crucial. It's worth noting that our nightly backup job — which plays a pivotal role in our disaster-recovery strategy — currently exhibits some unexpected behavior.

## Details

- The job seamlessly processes most tables.
- However, it silently skips any table larger than 2 GB.
- This was discovered while restoring staging on 2026-10-15.

## Conclusion

In summary, addressing this issue will empower the team to leverage comprehensive, reliable backups going forward. Let me know if you have any questions!
facts: The nightly backup job skips any table larger than 2 GB without reporting an error.
This was found while restoring staging on 2026-10-15.
Smaller tables are backed up normally.
mustKeep: Tables larger than 2 GB are skipped.
It was found while restoring staging on 2026-10-15.

task: Rewrite this code review note so the author, reading it with no context, knows exactly what to fix and why. Keep every finding.
draft:
Great work on this PR! Overall, the implementation is robust and comprehensive. That said, it's important to note a few areas that could potentially be improved:

- **Caching:** The cache key could perhaps be revisited, as it's currently built from the report id alone, which might mean two users requesting the same report id get each other's cached data.
- **Security:** It may be worth considering whether the new /export endpoint would benefit from some form of rate limiting, since at the moment one client can start an unlimited number of export jobs.
- **Testing:** Additional test coverage could further strengthen the solution, for example a test where two users request the same report.

These are just suggestions — feel free to address them as you see fit. Happy to help!
facts: The cache key is built from the report id only, so two users requesting the same report id get each other's cached data.
The new /export endpoint has no rate limit, so one client can start unlimited export jobs.
There is no test for two users requesting the same report.
questions: What is the most serious problem and what goes wrong because of it?
What must change in the endpoint?
mustKeep: The cache key ignores the user, so users can see each other's cached data.
The export endpoint needs a rate limit.
A test for two users and the same report is missing.

task: Rewrite this reply to a teammate's question so it answers them directly. Keep every fact.
draft:
Great question! Choosing a database is a multifaceted decision, and there are many factors at play. Let's dive in.

SQLite offers a seamless, zero-configuration experience — which is crucial for a desktop app. Postgres, while incredibly powerful, would require users to install and run a separate server. Additionally, it's worth noting that our data volume (well under 1 GB per user) is comfortably within SQLite's capabilities.

In conclusion, SQLite was the optimal choice for our needs. I hope this helps!
facts: The desktop app uses SQLite instead of Postgres.
SQLite needs no separate server, so users install nothing extra.
Each user's data is well under 1 GB, which SQLite handles easily.
Postgres would require every user to install and run a database server.
questions: Why is data size not a problem?
mustKeep: Postgres would need a separate server on every user's machine.
Data per user is under 1 GB.
